mul8's first operand, doubled as mul8 runs: music_note stores r1, the note length in units, here.
mul8's second operand, halved as mul8 runs: music_note stores r2, the release fraction, here. $47A2-$47A9 after it are zero and unreferenced.

A counter kept here for code in another range, the handlers at $9593-$9683 (a phase machine switched on $68): set to 10 at $959A and counted down at $95A6, which sets body frame 8 ($9363) when it reaches 0; also incremented at $967B, whose callers test its low three bits.

A count for the handlers at $9303-$9368 (another range): set at $9324 from the table at $932F, indexed by $0369 AND 7 (plus 8 when $0369 is negative), or 2 when $037B is set, and to 1 at $AB09. Every 32 passes (count_933f) $935E takes one off and sets body frame $20; at 0 the phase ends ($9327).

A pass counter for the handler at $933F (another range): incremented on every pass; the handler does nothing unless its low three bits are 0, and counts count_9324 down only when its low five bits are 0.
State for the handlers at $A88F-$A918 (another range): bits 0-1 select body frame $23 + n (set through $9363 at $A8DA), bit 7 the direction in which $A8C4 steps them; cleared at $A899.
A countdown for the handlers at $A88F-$A918: set to a random 64-255 at $A894, decremented at $A8F3 when the handler acts, cleared at $A8AE when $8F86 reports a pending request.
A pass counter for the handler at $A8A7-$A918: incremented at $A8B1 on every pass; the handler acts only when its low three bits are 0. $47B1-$47BF after it are zero and unreferenced.

Sprite shape $1F (VIC bank 1: $4000 + $1F * 64), authored, the same in the load image: 63 bytes, empty except rows 15-19, a small dotted wedge that widens downwards (2, 4, 6, 10 and 12 dots): the text cursor. The only store of $1F to a sprite pointer found in the traced code is at $0786, where the raster interrupt borrows a hardware sprite for the cursor (cursor_sprite_save, $0836): while $0710 or $0711 is set it shows this shape hires, dark grey ($0B), at Y = $35 and X = text_cursor_x + 13, the print position in the text band.

Sixteen 64-byte sprite shape buffers, VIC pointers $20-$2F ($4800-$4BFF), filled at run time by unpack_figure_sprite ($0E41), which unpacks a figure's frame into block $0D68,X after flipping that block number with EOR #$08 ($0EA3; also $1587), so the figures are double-buffered between $20-$27 and $28-$2F; $1396 turns a block number n into $4000 + 64 * n in $1A/$1B. The crack screen's code sits here in the load image, and the cold start zeroes $4800-$4FFF ($04A2-$04B5). In play-02 the pointers ($5FF8) are $21 $2A $2B $20 $24 $26 $25 $27.

Byte 8 of sprite shape buffer $25 ($4940-$497F). The only reference is ROL $4948,X at $AA6F, which is script data decoded as code (the bytes after $AA6B are a list of activity numbers), not a real access.

Unused as far as found: the cold start zeroes $4800-$4FFF ($04A2-$04B5) and $4C00-$4FFF stays zero in time-prompt, play-01 and play-02 (it held the crack screen's data before). No instruction names it; as sprite blocks $30-$3F it would need pointers the figures never use ($0D68 flips within $20-$2F).

The font for all on-screen text: 91 glyphs of 8 bytes for ASCII $20-$7A (space to 'z') in order, $5000-$52D7. The next byte, $52D8, is code (the entry of activity 32), so $7B-$7F have no glyph: printing one would draw code bytes. Byte 0 of a glyph is its metrics: low nibble = width in pixels, the advance (3 for space, 2 for 'i', 8 for 'M'); high nibble = rows to drop the glyph (1 for , ; Q j and 2 for g p q y, the descenders). Bytes 1-7 are its seven pixel rows, left-aligned. print_char's glyph fetch ($BB29) copies the 8 bytes at base + (char - $20) * 8 to $92-$99, the width to $90 and the drop plus $8E to $91; the base is the first entry of the table at $BDC0/$BDC2 ($5000). The second base, $5800, used for characters with bit 7 set, points at code in this build (letter and computer code).

Activity 32 ($20), its entry in activity_table ($8E09): the eating part of a meal. It is the third activity of the script at $AA56 ($3C, $2B, $20, $37, $3B) that activity $4A sets up, and the handler at $308C switches to it ($30A0) when food_need is 2 or more and the food store $30B4 is full. Each pass increments meal_ticks, then switches on activity_phase through act32_phases: walk to place $25 ($30CD: 4 further right when bit 0 of the food slot $30B2 is set); show figure 3 (frame $15) on the ground floor; carry figure 2 (frame $07) by places $26, $27 and $28; body frame $22; then rounds of eating (meal_rounds): bites with body frames $48/$47 and the head's frames $18, then $08, $19, $08, $1A, figure 2 raised to him and back; every bite resets food_need. Then back by places $27, $26 and $24 carrying figure 2, body frame $21, figures 2 and 3 hidden, script_next. A pending request (request_pending) ends the eating early.

Activity 32's switch table (JSR $3F11 at $52DB, on activity_phase): 28 handler addresses minus one. Phase 0 $30CD (walk to place $25), 1 meal_wait_arrival, 2 meal_show_fig3, 3 meal_walk_26, 4 $293D (carry until he stops), 5 meal_walk_27, 6 $293D, 7 meal_walk_28, 8 $293D, 9 meal_at_place_28, 10 meal_begin_eating, 11 meal_hide_fig3, 12 meal_bite, 13 meal_bite_wait, 14 meal_chew, 15 meal_check, 16 meal_show_fig3, 17 meal_at_place_28, 18 meal_walk_27, 19 $293D, 20 meal_walk_26, 21 $293D, 22 meal_walk_24, 23 $293D, 24 meal_stand, 25 meal_hide_fig3, 26 meal_done, 27 script_next.

Activity 32 phase 24, also activity 34's phase 2 (the dog's food, table at $280A): calls $255B (another range) with A = $21 and X = the person's facing ($039A), which moves the body to frame $21 over several passes and holds $2540 non-zero meanwhile; next phase once $2540 is 0.
Activity 32's rounds of eating left: set to a random 4-31 ($195E AND $1F, OR 4, so bit 2 is always set) by meal_begin_eating; meal_check takes one off every 16 passes and ends the eating at 0.

Activity 32's pass counter: incremented on every pass of the activity ($52D8) and never reset; its low bits pace meal_at_place_28 (every 8), meal_chew (a head frame every 8, bits 3-4 choosing it) and meal_check (every 16).
Activity 32's pause after a bite: set to 10 by meal_bite and counted down one a pass by meal_bite_wait.

Common tail of the meal's walk handlers: $2783 = 5, then on to $28F0 (another range), which gives figure 2 frame $07 (entry 5 of $2A4A) and $1394 = 7 (entry 5 of $2A5A), copies the person's place to it (copy_position), sets $0391 (the body's carrying frames) and moves to the next phase; the $293D phase that follows keeps figure 2 with him until he stops.

Activity 32 phases 9 and 17, at place $28: body frame $22 (set through $1ADF); figure 2 gets frame $13 and is hidden ($03C6 = 0) unless it already has that frame; then waits until meal_ticks AND 7 is 0 before the next phase.
Activity 32 phase 26: hides figure 2 ($03C6 = 0) and clears $0391 (no more carrying frames); next phase, which is script_next.
Activity 32 phase 1: waits until the person has stopped at place $25 ($03BC = 0), then next phase.

Walk to place $22 carrying figure 2, built like the four handlers after it. Nothing refers to $5366: act32_phases does not list it and no other table, jump or branch to it was found (searched for $65 $53 and $66 $53).
Activity 32 phase 22: walk to place $24 (ground floor, X 48) carrying figure 2 (X = $24, then the shared code at $5378).
Activity 32 phases 5 and 18: walk to place $27 (ground floor, X 60) carrying figure 2.
Activity 32 phase 7: walk to place $28 (ground floor, X 67), where he eats, carrying figure 2.

Activity 32 phases 3 and 20: walk to place $26 (ground floor, X 54) carrying figure 2. $5378, shared by the five walk handlers, calls walk_to_place with the place in X, takes back its phase advance (DEC activity_phase) and goes on to meal_carry.
Activity 32 phases 11 and 25, also activity 29's phase 17 (the drink of water, table at $37EA): hides figure 3 ($03C7 = 0), next phase.

Activity 32 phases 2 and 16, also activity 29's phase 2 (the drink of water, table at $37EA): shows figure 3 with frame $15 ($038E) at X $80 ($03AA, high bit $03AE = 0), floor Y $E5 (the ground floor, $03B2), depth 9 ($03B6), facing 0 ($039D), flags $83 ($03C7); also $1395 = 1 and $0395 = $FF; next phase.

Activity 32 phase 15, acting every 16 passes (meal_ticks AND 15 = 0): when a request is pending (request_pending) or meal_rounds is 0, sets $3579 = $FF, lets the head move again ($ACF1 = 0) and moves on to the walk back; otherwise takes one off meal_rounds and, when a random number AND 15 is below 7, goes back to phase 12 (meal_bite) for another bite, else waits another 16 passes.

Activity 32 phase 14, after a bite: puts figure 2 back at the person's floor Y (flags $81 when it moves) and the body back to frame $47 (flags $82); every 8 passes gives the head the frame from meal_head_frames chosen by bits 3-4 of meal_ticks. At the start of each 32-pass cycle it moves on to meal_check with a chance of 2 in 8 (always when meal_ticks is 0); otherwise it keeps chewing.
The head's frames while chewing, indexed by bits 3-4 of meal_ticks (meal_chew): $08, $19, $08, $1A.

Activity 32 phase 12, a bite: sets $3578 = $FF, clears letter_done ($54E2) and food_need ($0371), reloads food_timer from food_period, calls $392F (reloads act4_countdown if it is 0; clears illness_worsening when both needs are below 3), sets meal_delay to 10, body frame $48 and head frame $18 (flags $82), raises figure 2 to four lines above the person's floor Y (flags $81), next phase.
Activity 32 phase 13: counts meal_delay down, one a pass, and moves on when it reaches 0.

Activity 32 phase 10, the eating begins: facing from bit 7 of person_facing_bit ($034A into $039A), meal_rounds = random 4-31, $03AD, $0398 and $037C cleared, $0394 and $ACF1 = $FF (the head's turning off), body frame $47, head frame $08, figure 2 frame $14 put on the person (his X and floor Y, depth one less), flags $83 for figure 2 and the body and $82 for the head, $1394 = 7; next phase.

Non-zero while the person types a letter: set to $FF by letter_type ($5728) for each character, cleared when the text band is cleared ($BAD6). While it is set, print_queued ends the line at the next space or '-' once the print position is past 255 (text_cursor_x_hi set), printing a new line instead of that character and calling letter_wrap ($BAA6); and the line editor ($3736) ignores the player's keys.
Lines of the letter typed so far, 1-8: 1 at letter_begin, raised by letter_count_line (at most 8); draw_typewriter shows that many pixel rows of paper above the typewriter.
The typewriter carriage position draw_typewriter last drew, 0-8 (text_cursor_x / 32, at most 8); it redraws only when this changes.

1 once a letter has been begun (letter_begin, $55B6); while it is set, activity 22 ends at once (letter_check), so he types no second letter. Cleared by every bite of a meal (meal_bite, $5444) and by the drink at $38C2: after eating or drinking he can write again.

Activity 22 ($16), its entry in activity_table: the person types a letter to the player, as asked with "type a letter" (the parser rules at $CA1A and $CA2A give action $16). Switches on activity_phase through act22_phases: stops at once if letter_done; if a record is playing, walks to it (place 1) and stops it ($924D-$926E); walks to the typewriter on the top floor (places 7 and 8), puts figure 2 (frame $11) beside it at X $E2, goes to place $0A, moves figure 2 to X $E7, goes to place 9 at the typewriter with his sprites behind the picture; then letter_begin, letter_compose and letter_type type the letter into the text band while the paper rises out of the typewriter; then clears the paper and goes back the same way, hiding figure 2, and script_next. A request pending as he arrives skips the typing.

Activity 22's switch table (JSR $3F11 at $54E3, on activity_phase): 30 handler addresses minus one. 0 letter_check, 1 $924D (to phase 7 when no record plays), 2 set_target_1, 3 $2F0A, 4 $928D, 5 $9297, 6 $926E (record off), 7 letter_walk_07, 8 wait_or_request, 9 letter_walk_08, 10 wait_or_request, 11 letter_fig2_e2, 12 letter_walk_0a, 13 letter_wait_sit, 14 letter_fig2_e7, 15 letter_walk_09, 16 letter_wait_sit, 17 letter_begin, 18 letter_compose, 19 letter_type, 20 letter_clear_paper, 21 letter_walk_0a, 22 letter_wait, 23 letter_fig2_e2, 24 letter_walk_08, 25 letter_wait, 26 letter_hide_fig2, 27 letter_walk_07, 28 letter_wait, 29 script_next.
Activity 22 phase 0: if letter_done is set, jumps to the last phase (activity_phase = $1D, script_next), so no second letter is typed; otherwise next phase.
Activity 22 phases 12 and 21: $ACF2 = 2 (steers the head, read at $ADDB), then walk to place $0A (top floor, X 113).
Activity 22 phases 7 and 27: walk to place 7 (top floor, X 96), near the typewriter. Its JMP walk_to_place at $5536 is shared by the other walk handlers here and by computer_walk.
Activity 22 phases 9 and 24: $0396 = 0 (the person's sprites in front of the picture again), then walk to place 8 (top floor, X 106).
Activity 22 phases 13 and 16: when a request is pending (request_pending) jumps to phase 20 (clear the paper and leave, no letter); otherwise waits until the person stops ($03BC = 0) and moves on.
Activity 22 phases 22, 25 and 28: waits until the person stops ($03BC = 0), then next phase.
Activity 22 phase 15: $0396 = 9, which puts the person's sprites behind the picture (read at $11E3 into the priority shadow $0D5D), then walk to place 9 (top floor, X 118), at the typewriter.
Activity 22 phase 14: moves figure 2 to X $E7 (letter_fig2_e2's code with that X).

Activity 22 phases 11 and 23: puts figure 2 at X $E2 ($03A9), floor Y $63 (the top floor, $03B1), depth 8 ($03B5), frame $11, facing 0 ($039C), $03AD = 0, $0398 = $63, $1394 = $0F, flags $83 and $0394 = $83: an object by the typewriter (not identified), which phase 14 moves to X $E7.
Activity 22 phase 26, also activity 91's phase 2 (table at $ABE4): hides figure 2 ($03C6 = 0, $0398 = 0), next phase.
Returns in A the next character of the letter, at letter_ptr ($66/$67), and advances letter_ptr.

Activity 22 phase 17: $ACF2 = $A2 (the head's turn), letter_ptr = $7F40 (the letter buffer), letter_lines = 1, letter_done = 1, opens the text band ($BA3A), body frame $2D (set_person_frame), next phase.

Activity 22 phase 18: builds the letter in the buffer at $7F40 (the record driver's work area, free once the record is off): txt_letter_dear; then txt_letter_thanks when both $30B4 (the food store, four bits; CTRL F asks for a delivery unless it is full, $2B54) and $2B51 (the water tank; CTRL W adds one, up to 11, $2C87) are non-zero, otherwise txt_letter_complaint; then txt_letter_signoff and $FF. The complaint letter is 158 characters and runs over sid_shadow ($7FCD-$7FDE), which music_start rewrites before the next record.
letter_compose's write index into the buffer at $7F40: 0 at the start, advanced by letter_copy_piece.
Copies the letter piece at $5600 + X, up to its byte with bit 7 set, to $7F40 + letter_write_index, and advances the index.
Letter text, ASCII, $0D for a new line, $FF at the end: "Dear Friend,", return, two spaces
Letter text, ASCII, $0D for a new line, $FF at the end: "Thank You," and "Your Friend", each indented eight spaces
Letter text, ASCII, $0D for a new line, $FF at the end: "Thank you for keeping me well stocked with food and water."
Letter text, ASCII, $0D for a new line, $FF at the end: "Please notice that my supplies are running low.  I can't stay happy and healthy without your support."
Passes to wait before the next character of the letter: 2 or 3 at random after each one ($573D), counted down by letter_type; it also indexes letter_type_frames.
The body frame letter_type set last, so that it calls set_person_frame only when the frame changes ($55 in the load image).
The body frames while typing, by letter_key_delay: 0 $2B (the pass a key is struck), 1 $2C, 2 $2D, 3 $2C.

Activity 22 phase 19, once a pass: draw_typewriter; returns while $BA36 or $BA37 is non-zero (text-band work print_queued still has to do, see $BAC8); sets the body frame from letter_type_frames and, when it changes, $039A to bit 3 of rng_value; counts letter_key_delay down; at 0 takes the next character (letter_next_char): $FF ends the phase; $0D also counts a line (letter_count_line); the character goes to the output queue (queue_char) with letter_typing set, a printable one also setting $355D (one-shot sound $0A, the one the line editor uses for keys); letter_key_delay is then 2 or 3.
Called by print_queued ($BAA6) when it breaks a line of the letter: sets $355C (one-shot sound $0B) and falls into letter_count_line.
Adds one to letter_lines, at most 8. Called for each $0D in the letter text and through letter_wrap.

Draws the typewriter's moving parts into the house bitmap. The carriage position is text_cursor_x / 32 (at most 8); when it differs from carriage_pos it redraws the top two pixel rows of bitmap row 6, columns 26-29 ($6850-$686F, the carriage) from carriage_cell26-29, and row 5, columns 26-29 ($6710-$672F, the paper) from paper_cell26-29, with only the bottom letter_lines pixel rows filled.

Paper pixels for bitmap row 5, column 26, indexed by the carriage position 0-8. The four paper_cell tables are 4 bytes apart in one 20-byte strip, $57C3-$57D6 = 00 00 00 00 00 00 03 0F 3F FF FF FF FC F0 C0 00 00 00 00 00, so each cell shows the strip 4 bytes (one cell) further on and the sheet slides left as the carriage position grows.
Paper pixels for bitmap row 5, column 27: the paper strip from its fifth byte, indexed by the carriage position (see paper_cell26).
Paper pixels for bitmap row 5, column 28: the paper strip from its ninth byte, indexed by the carriage position.
Paper pixels for bitmap row 5, column 29: the paper strip from its thirteenth byte, indexed by the carriage position.

Carriage pixels for the top two pixel rows of bitmap row 6, column 26, indexed by the carriage position 0-8. The four carriage_cell tables are 4 bytes apart in one 20-byte strip, $57D7-$57EA = 00 00 00 00 00 03 0F 3F FF FF FF FF FF FC F0 C0 00 00 00 00: a solid bar with soft ends that slides left as the carriage position grows.
Carriage pixels for bitmap row 6, column 27: the carriage strip from its fifth byte, indexed by the carriage position (see carriage_cell26).
Carriage pixels for bitmap row 6, column 28: the carriage strip from its ninth byte, indexed by the carriage position.
Carriage pixels for bitmap row 6, column 29: the carriage strip from its thirteenth byte, indexed by the carriage position.

Puts the typewriter back as the picture has it: clears all eight pixel rows of bitmap row 5, columns 25-29 ($6708-$672F, the paper) and redraws the top two pixel rows of row 6, columns 25-29: $FF at columns 27-28 (the carriage at rest), 0 elsewhere. Called by letter_clear_paper and when the text band is cleared ($BAFE).
Activity 22 phase 20: clear_typewriter, next phase.
Sets the person's body frame to A: X = 0, then JMP $1ADF. Used by the letter ($55BE, $56FD) and computer ($584E, $58D8) handlers.

Activity 20 ($14), its entry in activity_table: the person uses the computer, as asked with "computer" (the parser rule at $CAFA gives action $14). Switches on activity_phase through act20_phases: walk to place $1E (middle floor, X 144, the desk with the computer drawn at bitmap rows 12-13, columns 36-38), wait_or_request, computer_sit, computer_run until his time is up or a request comes, script_next. The monitor shows one of two programs, chosen at random: lines of dots that scroll up as he types, or a drawing (bar chart, wandering dot or scribble) on a 7 x 9 grid of multicolour pixels.
Activity 20's switch table (JSR $3F11 at $5825), handler addresses minus one: 0 computer_walk, 1 wait_or_request, 2 computer_sit, 3 computer_run, 4 script_next.
Activity 20 phase 0: walk to place $1E (middle floor, X 144), the computer desk (X = $1E, then JMP $5536, walk_to_place).
computer_run's pass counter, incremented every pass; computer_run acts only on the passes where it AND computer_pace is 0.
How long he stays at the computer: a random $20-$FF from computer_sit, counted down on computer_run's acting passes; at 0 he stops. Zeroed when a request is pending.
Acting passes to sit still: 20 at the start (computer_sit), then a random 0-15 after each body frame $1D; while it counts down computer_run does nothing else.

Activity 20 phase 2: $ACF2 = $4A (the head's turn), computer_pause = 20, computer_time = random $20-$FF, body frame $1D, computer_program (picks a program and blanks the screen), computer_pace = random 3 or 7, next phase.
computer_run's pace mask, a random 3 or 7 (random AND 7, OR 3): it acts on one pass in 4 or one in 8.
$1A on a pass where computer_run gave the body frame $1A, 0 on every other pass; with computer_key_1d it tells the text program to put the next dot of the line on the screen.

$1D from the acting pass where computer_run gives the body frame $1D (a pause) until the first acting pass after the pause, which clears it. While it is set, computer_text_step adds a dot on every pass, so lines pour out and scroll while he sits back.

Activity 20 phase 3, every pass. On acting passes (computer_ticks AND computer_pace = 0): a pending request zeroes computer_time; computer_pause counts down first; when computer_time is 0 it blanks the screen (computer_blank), sets $3571 = 2 and $ACF2 = 2 and moves on; otherwise it takes one off computer_time and moves the body: from frame $1B to $1A (random facing, $039A = bit 3) or, 1 time in 8, to $1D with a pause of 0-15; from any other frame to $1B, with the key sound ($355D) in the text program. Then the screen: computer_draw in the drawing program, computer_text_step in the text program.
Common exit of the screen work: when main_passes ($09DB) is 0 and a random number is below $0F, calls computer_program to switch programs at random.

The text program's step: when computer_key_1a or computer_key_1d is set, adds the next dot to the bottom line of the monitor, writing screen_char_pixels at $7160 + screen_char_offsets for dot plot_y of plot_x; when the line is full (plot_y = plot_x) it scrolls instead (computer_scroll) and starts a new line.
The text program's seven dots, the byte each one changes, as offsets from $7160 (bitmap row 13, column 36): 3, $0B, $0B, $0B, $0B, $13, $13, i.e. pixel row 3 of columns 36, 37 (four times) and 38.

The value computer_text_step writes for each of the seven dots: $12, $80, $A0, $A8, $AA, $81, $A1: one more multicolour pixel of colour 2 each time, left to right along the bottom line inside the monitor's frame.

The text program's line feed: scrolls the picture inside the monitor up one pixel row (pixel rows 3-7 of bitmap row 12 and 0-3 of row 13, columns 36-38), redraws the empty bottom line ($10, $00, $01: just the frame's edges), and starts a new line of random length 0-7 (plot_x) with plot_y = 0. Brackets its writes with the empty hooks $5B2A and $5B29.
The drawing canvas's x (0-6) to an AND mask clearing that multicolour pixel: $FC, $3F, $CF, $F3, $FC, $3F, $CF (the last pixel of column 36, all four of column 37, the first two of column 38).
Canvas x (0-6) to its cell's byte offset: 0, 8, 8, 8, 8, $10, $10 (bitmap columns 36, 37 and 38).
Canvas y (0-8, bottom up) to its pixel row: $83, $82, $81, $80 (rows 3-0 of bitmap row 13; bit 7 selects the $7160 base), then 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 (rows of bitmap row 12, base $7020).
The four multicolour values filling a whole byte: $00, $55, $AA, $FF; plot_pixel keeps the bits of the one pixel being painted.
The x step of each of the drawing pen's eight directions: 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, -1, -1, -1 ($59A2 + d).
The y step of each of the eight directions: 1, 1, 0, -1, -1, -1, 0, 1 ($59A4 + d; it overlaps pen_dx by six bytes).
The drawing pen's x on the canvas, 0-6.
The drawing pen's y on the canvas, 0-8 (0 at the bottom).
The colour (0-3, an index into screen_colours) that plot_pixel paints with.
plot_pixel's scratch: the colour's bits for the pixel being painted.
The computer's program: 0 the text program, 1 the drawing program; chosen at random by computer_program.
plot_pixel's x (0-6); in the text program the length of the current line of dots (0-7, 3 after computer_blank).
plot_pixel's y (0-8); in the text program the number of dots already on the line.

The drawing program's style, from computer_program: 0 a bar chart; otherwise a random value AND $87, OR 1, where bit 7 set is a scribble that keeps its trail and bit 7 clear a single wandering dot, and the low bits (ANDed with main_passes) pace it.
The bar chart's current colour, 1-3, chosen at random at every second column.
The bar chart's current bar height, 2-9 at random, at which the pen moves to the next column; 1 once the seventh bar is done.

The drawing program, from computer_run when computer_mode is 1; acts only when main_passes AND draw_style AND $7F is 0. Style 0, the bar chart: one pixel every 16 passes, filling columns bottom-up to bar_height in bar_colour; after the seventh column it may switch program (1 time in 16). Other styles: the pen takes one step in a random direction (pen_dx, pen_dy, kept on the canvas) and paints a random colour 1-3; with bit 7 of draw_style clear the old position is erased first, so it is a wandering dot, with it set a scribble.

Paints canvas pixel (plot_x, plot_y) in pen_colour: the byte is at screen_x_cells + the row from screen_y_rows, from $7020 or, when bit 7 is set, $7160; the pixel's bits (screen_x_masks) are replaced with the colour's (screen_colours). Brackets the write with the empty hooks $5B2A and $5B29.

Picks the computer's program at random: computer_mode = a random bit. Text program: sound flag $3571 = 1. Drawing program: sound flag $3570 = 1 and draw_style = 0 or, half the time, a random style. Then pen and plot positions to 0 and computer_blank.
Blanks the monitor: plot_x = 3 and pixel rows 3-7 of bitmap row 12 and 0-3 of row 13, columns 36-38, set to $10, $00 and $01, the empty screen with its side edges.
An RTS: an empty hook called after bitmap writes, at $0CE5 (draw_clock_hand), $5968 (computer_scroll) and $5ACD (plot_pixel). Why it is there is not known.
An RTS: an empty hook called before bitmap writes, at $0CC7 (draw_clock_hand), $5921 (computer_scroll) and $5AA6 (plot_pixel). Why it is there is not known.

Activity 113 ($71), its entry in activity_table ($8EAB): walk to place $16 (middle floor, X 90), wait_or_request, body frame $45, then figure 2 is put on the person and stepped through frames $0E, $0F, $10, $0F every fourth pass for a random 64-255 steps, with the sound flag $3565 set and the head held still; then figure 2 is hidden, body frame $5C, sound flag $3569, script_next. What it shows is not known, and nothing that starts it was found: no parser rule, activity script or store of $71 to activity names it.
Activity 113's switch table (JSR $3F11 at $5B2B), handler addresses minus one: 0 walk_to_place_16, 1 wait_or_request, 2 act113_turn, 3 act113_start, 4 act113_animate, 5 act113_end, 6 script_next.
RTS: the exit act113_turn takes while $255B is still changing the body frame ($2540 non-zero).
Activity 113 phase 2: $ACF1 = $FF (head held still), then $255B with A = $45 and X = 0 moves the body to frame $45; next phase once $2540 is 0.

Activity 113 phase 3: copy_position to figure 2, one less in $03B5 (its depth), $ACF1 = $FF, sound flag $3565 = $FF, $0394 = $FF, $1394 = 1, $03F4 = $0F (the head's direction), frame $0F for figure 2 (flags $83) and for the head (flags $82), act113_time = random $40-$FF, next phase.
Activity 113 phase 5: $ACF1 = 0 (the head free again), figure 2 hidden ($03C6 = 0), body frame $5C (through $9363), sound flag $3569 = $FF, next phase.
Activity 113's length: a random $40-$FF from act113_start, counted down on act113_animate's acting passes.
act113_animate's step counter; its low two bits pick the frame from act113_frames.

Activity 113 phase 4: waits until figure 2's last frame is drawn ($03C6 AND 3 = 0) and acts every fourth pass (main_passes AND 3 = 0): moves on when a request is pending or act113_time runs out; otherwise steps act113_step and gives figure 2 the next frame from act113_frames (flags $82).
Figure 2's frames in act113_animate, a cycle of four: $0E, $0F, $10, $0F.

Copies the person's (figure 0's) position to figure X: X high bit $03AB, X $03A7, half X $03A3 (rebuilt from those two), floor Y $03AF, depth $03B3 and facing $039A. Called with X = 2 at $290B (carrying) and by act113_start.
Eight bytes $00 $FF $00 $FF $00 $FF $00 $FF after copy_position, the same in the load image; no reference found. Not known to be used.

The house picture: a multicolour bitmap of 25 character rows by 40 columns, 320 bytes a row (8 bytes a cell, top line first), $6000-$7F3F, shown through VIC bank 1 with its colours in the matrix at $5C00 and in colour RAM. It is authored data loaded with the program: between crack-screen.vsf and play-02.vsf only three bytes of the clock's hands ($6D95, $6D96, $6D9F) differ. Rows 0-2 are the text band above the roof, rows 2-7 the roof and the attic, rows 8-16 the middle storey (bedroom, stairs, bathroom, study) and rows 16-24 the ground floor (kitchen, stairs, living room). Besides the spots described at their own labels, draw_object ($96ED) redraws 16 house objects (doors, drawers, cupboards, the fire, the player's petting arm and hand) at the positions in obj_bmp_lo/hi ($9873/$9883); the row labels name them by object number. This first row: every byte is $55, so while no text is shown the band is solid colour 6, blue ($62 in the colour matrix). $BAD4 refills rows 0-1 with $55 when the band's timer $0710 runs out; $BDA2 clears rows 0-2 to 0 (colours $0C) before text is printed, and the raster IRQ then turns multicolour off above the band's bottom ($0711) so the text shows in hi-res. The label is also the base of the store at $31B8, which is rewritten at run time to address the kitchen cupboard (rows 19-20).
Row 0, columns 8-31 of the text band: $55 fill while idle; print_char ($BB08, address from $BBEE) draws the typed line and the letters here in hi-res.

Row 0, columns 32-39 ($6100-$613F): end of the band's first row, $55. $6100 is the second page of the 256-byte loops in $BAD4 ($BAE0: $55) and $BDA2 ($BDB3: 0), which clear $6000-$63BF a page at a time.
Row 1, columns 0-15: the band's second row, $55 in every byte (blue) while no text is shown; a text line when the band is in use.
Row 1, columns 16-23 ($61C0-$61FF), $55. $61C0 is the base of $BAD4's third store ($BAE3), which fills $61C0-$62BF with $55: the rest of row 1 and columns 0-7 of row 2.
Row 1, columns 24-31 ($6200-$623F), $55. $6200 is the base of $BDA2's third store ($BDB6), which zeroes $6200-$62FF.
Row 1, columns 32-39: the right end of the band's second row, $55 fill (blue sky beside the roof).
Row 2, columns 0-7: sky left of the roof ($55), cleared with the rest of the band.
Last byte of row 2, column 7 (sky, $55). $62BF is the base of $BDA2's last store ($BDB9), which zeroes $62BF-$63BE: the rest of row 2, where the roof ridge is.

Row 2, columns 8-15 ($62C0-$62FF): the start of the roof's top row, the left slope rising to the flat ridge. $62C0-$63BF (columns 8-39 of row 2) is identical to the 256 bytes at $BDD0, which $BAD4 ($BAE6-$BAE9) copies back here after text has blanked the band.

Row 2, columns 16-39: the roof ridge (a brown line to about column 29), the right slope starting down (columns 30-31), black attic below and blue sky right of it; from $BDD0+$40 when $BAD4 restores it.

Row 3: under the roof: the two roof slopes (brown diagonals, about columns 7-8 and 31-32) with blue sky outside them, the black attic between, and the top of the upstairs closet's white door (columns 22-24; object 5, rows 3-7, which draw_object ($96ED) redraws as it opens and closes).
Row 4: the roof slopes further out (about columns 5-6 and 33-34), sky outside, the upstairs closet door (columns 22-24, object 5).
Row 5, columns 0-8: the left roof slope and the television's aerial (columns 4-6), then the left side of the stereo cabinet (columns 7-8).

Row 5, columns 9-10 ($6688-$6697): the record on the stereo's turntable. While turntable_on ($2B45) is set, $2DBB copies one of four 16-byte frames from $2D72 here every eighth main-loop pass ($96DD counts 0-3), moving a gap along the record's edge so it seems to turn; $2DB2 puts frame 0 back when stereo_off stops the music.
Row 5, columns 11-24: the right side of the stereo, the top of the purple armchair's back (about column 14), the green piano (columns 17-20) and the upstairs closet door (columns 22-24, object 5).

Row 5, column 25 ($6708-$670F): left edge of the space above the typewriter where the sheet of paper appears while he types a letter. $57EB clears it (and the rest of the paper area) to 0; the paper drawing at $5760 only writes columns 26-29.

Row 5, column 26: part of the typewriter's sheet of paper. $5760 draws the sheet, eight lines of the patterns at $57C3-$57CF picked by the carriage position ($5756: from the print cursor $8C/$8D, 0-8), showing only the bottom $54E0 lines (one more per typed line, up to 8); $57EB blanks it.
Row 5, column 27: the sheet of paper in the typewriter, second column (pattern table $57C7).
Row 5, column 28: the sheet of paper in the typewriter, third column (pattern table $57CB).
Row 5, column 29: the sheet of paper in the typewriter, fourth column (pattern table $57CF).
Row 5, columns 30-39: black attic right of the paper, the green filing cabinet (columns 32-34) and the right roof slope with sky outside.

Row 6, columns 0-24: the attic's furniture at floor level: the television set (columns 4-5; while tv_on ($2B4A) is set, $2D59 gives its screen cells a random colour in colour RAM at $D8F5/$D91D every fourth pass), the stereo cabinet with its speaker grille (columns 7-11), the purple armchair (columns 12-14), the green piano with its stool (columns 17-21) and the upstairs closet door (columns 22-24, object 5).
Row 6, column 25, lines 0-1 ($6848-$6849): the typewriter below the paper; $57EB sets them to 0. Lines 2-7 are the typewriter and desk, never changed.

Row 6, column 26, lines 0-1: the left end of the typewriter's purple carriage. $5760 redraws lines 0-1 of columns 26-29 from $57D7, $57DB, $57DF and $57E3 at the carriage position, so the carriage slides as he types; $57EB puts back the resting typewriter (this cell 0).
Row 6, column 27, lines 0-1: the typewriter's carriage (from $57DB; $FF, solid, in the resting state set by $57EB).
Row 6, column 28, lines 0-1: the typewriter's carriage (from $57DF; $FF at rest).
Row 6, column 29, lines 0-1: the right end of the typewriter's carriage (from $57E3; 0 at rest).

Row 6, columns 30-39: the right end of the typing desk (to column 31), the filing cabinet's drawer (columns 32-34, rows 6-7: object 11, drawn closed, half open or open by draw_object ($96ED)) and the right roof slope.

Row 7: the attic floor: grey rugs, the yellow rug under the stereo (columns 7-10), the foot of the closet door (object 5), the legs of the typing desk (columns 25-31), the lower part of the filing-cabinet drawer (object 11) and the lower ends of the roof at both sides.
Row 8: the thick floor between the attic and the storey below: the lower edge of the attic's grey rug along the top (columns 0-18) and brown below.
Row 9: the top of the upper storey: black walls, the side walls (columns 0 and 39), the wall between bathroom and study (column 30) and the top of the stairs to the attic (columns 20-22).
Row 10, columns 0-33: the stairs to the attic (about columns 19-22) and the upper rim of the wall clock in the study (column 33).

Row 10, columns 34-35 ($6D90-$6D9F): the upper middle of the study's wall clock. draw_wall_clock ($0AAC) copies a clean face here from clock_face_top ($0D1A), then draw_clock_hand ($0C5A) clears pixels (AND at $0CCE-$0CD3) along each hand, so these are the only bitmap bytes that differ between the crack-screen and play-02 snapshots.
Row 10, columns 36-39: the clock's right rim and the wall above the computer.

Row 11, columns 0-33: the tops of the bedroom closet's white door (columns 9-11, object 4, rows 11-15) and the dresser's mirror (columns 12-15), the stairs (columns 16-22), the mirror cabinet over the bathroom sink (columns 21-22, object 6, rows 11-13), the bathroom door (columns 23-25, object 3, rows 11-15), the shower pipe (columns 26-29), the bookcase (columns 30-32) and the clock's left rim. The three objects are redrawn by draw_object ($96ED) when they open.

Row 11, columns 34-35 ($6ED0-$6EDF): the lower middle of the wall clock, copied from clock_face_bottom ($0D2A) by draw_wall_clock before draw_clock_hand clears the pixels of hands pointing below the centre ($0CDD-$0CE2).
Row 11, columns 36-39: the clock's lower rim and the top of the computer's monitor (columns 36-38).

Row 12, columns 0-35: the bed's green headboard (columns 1-6), the bedroom closet door (object 4), the dresser's mirror, the stair banister, the mirror cabinet (object 6), the bathroom door (object 3), the shower, the bookcase and the top of the computer desk.

Row 12, column 36 ($7020-$7027): the left third of the computer's screen. With rows 12-13 of columns 36-38 it forms a 9-line display (lines 3-7 here, 0-3 in row 13) that activity 20 (the computer, $5825-$5B28) fills with dots: $5A8E plots them (AND/ORA at $5AB4/$5ABA) and $5921-$5984 scrolls the display up a line. Also the base for column 36 in the plot.
Row 12, column 36, line 1: source of the screen scroll's copy loop ($5926 reads $7021+X, X = 3-6, into $7020+X), i.e. lines 4-7 move up to 3-6.
Row 12, column 36, line 3: top line of the computer screen's display area; $5AFF blanks it with $10 (the screen's left edge).
Row 12, column 36, line 4: second line of the computer display; $5AFF also writes $10 here (it stores to $7024+X as well as $7023+X).
Row 12, column 36, line 7: the screen scroll copies row 13's line 0 ($7160) up into this line ($5940).
Row 12, column 37 ($7028-$702F): the middle third of the computer screen (scroll loop destination at $592F).
Row 12, column 37, line 1: source of the middle column's scroll copy ($592C).
Row 12, column 37, line 3: top line of the display's middle column, blanked to 0 by $5AFF ($5B14).
Row 12, column 37, line 4: blanked to 0 with line 3 by $5AFF ($5B17).
Row 12, column 37, line 7: receives row 13 column 37's line 0 ($7168) in the scroll ($5946).
Row 12, column 38 ($7030-$7037): the right third of the computer screen (scroll destination at $5935).
Row 12, column 38, line 1: source of the right column's scroll copy ($5932).
Row 12, column 38, line 3: top line of the display's right column, set to 1 (the screen's right edge) by $5AFF ($5B1F).
Row 12, column 38, line 4: set to 1 with line 3 by $5AFF ($5B22).
Row 12, column 38, line 7: receives row 13 column 38's line 0 ($7170) in the scroll ($594C). The next 8 bytes are column 39, the study's right wall.
Row 13, columns 0-6: the bed's green headboard (columns 1-6) against the wall.

Row 13, column 7, lines 1-7 ($7079-$707F): the left half of the alarm clock on the bedroom nightstand. While the alarm rings (CTRL A, or the morning alarm of daily_schedule) $2A79 counts $2B4F down and every fourth call ($2A8D) copies seven bytes from $2AB1 here, starting one byte later when bit 2 of $2B4F is set, so the bell jumps a line up and down.
Row 13, column 8, lines 1-7 ($7081-$7087): the right half of the alarm clock, from $2AB9 in the same animation.

Row 13, columns 9-35: the bedroom closet door (object 4), the dresser, the stairs, the sink under the mirror cabinet (object 6's last row), the bathroom door (object 3), the shower, the bookcase with its cupboard (columns 30-31, rows 13-15, object 13) and the computer keyboard on the desk (about columns 33-35).

Row 13, column 36 ($7160-$7167): lower-left part of the computer screen (display lines 5-8 are this cell's lines 0-3). Plot target when the row index's bit 7 is set ($5AC4/$5ACA), scroll destination ($5954); $5B06 blanks it to $10; $590B, indexed from here by $5913 (3, $0B, $13), writes the pattern bytes at $591A into the display's bottom line ($7163, $716B, $7173).
Row 13, column 36, line 1: source of the lower screen's scroll copy ($5951: lines 1-3 move up to 0-2).
Row 13, column 36, line 3: bottom line of the computer display; after each scroll $596D writes $10 (a blank line with the left edge) here.
Row 13, column 37 ($7168-$716F): lower middle of the computer screen: scroll source for the line above ($5943) and destination ($595A); $5B11 blanks it.
Row 13, column 37, line 1: source of the middle column's lower scroll copy ($5957).
Row 13, column 37, line 3: bottom line of the display's middle column, zeroed after each scroll ($5972).
Row 13, column 38 ($7170-$7177): lower right of the computer screen: scroll source ($5949) and destination ($5960); $5B1C sets it to 1.
Row 13, column 38, line 1: source of the right column's lower scroll copy ($595D).
Row 13, column 38, line 3: bottom line of the display's right column, set to 1 (right edge) after each scroll ($5979). Bytes $7174-$717F are the monitor's frame and column 39.

Row 14: the lower part of the middle storey's furniture: the bed, the nightstand's drawer (columns 6-8, object 9), the feet of the closet and bathroom doors (objects 4 and 3), the dresser's drawer (columns 12-16, object 10), the foot of the stairs, the sink's stand, the bathtub, the bookcase cupboard (object 13), the computer desk and its chair. The drawers are redrawn by draw_object ($96ED).

Row 15: the middle storey's floor: the bed's checked blanket (columns 1-7), the bedroom floor, the bathroom's checked floor (columns 20-29) and the study's green carpet (columns 30-38); the bottom rows of objects 3, 4 and 13 (the two doors and the bookcase cupboard) reach into it.

Row 16: the front edge of the upper floor, which is also the ground floor's ceiling: the bed's green frame (columns 0-7), the yellow rug (columns 8-15), the bathroom's checks and the study's green carpet, brown elsewhere.
Row 17: the top of the ground floor: the cord of the kitchen's hanging lamp (column 15) and the top of the stairs down (columns 17-19).

Row 18: kitchen and living room, upper walls: a white shelf (columns 0-1), the top of the food cupboard (columns 5-8), the window's awning (columns 9-11), the lamp cord, the stairs (columns 17-19), and the top of the picture on the living-room wall (columns 32-35).

Row 18, column 38, lines 2-7, and column 39: black wall above the front door and the house's right wall. No instruction addresses $77B2: the symbol comes from the sound-job table at $399C being read as four low/high pairs ($B2, the low byte of job 3 at $45B2, paired with $77, the low byte of job 7 at $4677), where it is eight low bytes followed by eight high bytes.

Row 19: the shelf, the refrigerator's upper door (columns 3-5, rows 19-21, object 1), the food cupboard's upper shelf, the window, the hanging lamp's shade (columns 14-15), the stairs, the shade of the living room's floor lamp (columns 30-31, coloured by $A93A through $5F16/$5F17), the picture and the top of the front door (columns 36-38, rows 19-23, object 0). The store at $31B8 is aimed at $77F0 and $77F8 (columns 6-7, lines 0-4): two of the four food packets in the cupboard, drawn with the $31CA pattern when their bits are set in $30B4 and cleared otherwise ($3198).

Row 20, columns 0-17: the refrigerator (its upper door, object 1, and the freezer door below, object 2, rows 20-23, both columns 3-5), the food cupboard's lower shelf (the other two food packets at $7930 and $7938, columns 6-7, drawn by $3198) and the window's lower half.

Row 20, column 18, lines 4-7 ($7994-$7997): the top four lines of the water cooler's bottle, left half. $2D0D redraws the bottle's 12 lines from the bottom up: the lowest $2B51 lines (the water: 0-11, one more per CTRL W press, $2C87-$2C97) as $AA, bit pairs %10 (the colour matrix's low-nibble colour), the rest as $55, %01 (its high-nibble colour), masked by $2D41.
Row 20, column 19, lines 4-7 ($799C-$799F): the right half of the water cooler bottle's top four lines (mask $2D4D).

Row 20, columns 20-39: the stairs; the player's petting arm (object 14, columns 23-28, reaching right toward the easy chair) and hand (object 15, columns 27-28), which draw_object ($96ED) draws from petting_anim; the pole of the floor lamp (column 30), the top of the fireplace (columns 32-35) and the front door (object 0).
Row 21, column 0: the house's left wall and the left edge of the stove, whose burners are at lines 6-7 of columns 1-2.

Row 21, column 1, line 0: the black space above the stove's burners. The handler at $1EA7 (in the switch tables of activities 48 and 49) stores 0 here, clears $7A49-$7A4C and $7A51 too, and sets the colour matrix of these two cells ($5F49/$5F4A) to $7F.
Row 21, column 1, lines 1-5 ($7A49-$7A4D): the stove top's left cell, lines 1-4 cleared by $1EBA; line 5 unchanged.

Row 21, column 1, line 6: the stove's burner. $2CD9, on every pass of the house updates, stores $2A while $2B52 is 0 and $EA while it is set: the left pixel pair then shows colour RAM $DB49, which $2CEB-$2D04 sets on alternate passes to a random entry of $2D08 (7, 6, 8, 6, 1: yellow, blue, orange, blue, white), never the same entry twice running: a flickering flame.
Row 21, column 2, line 1: the stove top's right cell, cleared by $1EC0 with the others. The rest of column 2 is stove.

Row 21, columns 3-16: the refrigerator (objects 1 and 2), the counter with the sink's taps (columns 6-11) and the kitchen cabinet door under it (columns 6-7, rows 21-23, object 12), and a small white object above the kitchen table (columns 14-15).

Row 21, column 17, line 4: index base of the water-level drawing ($2D23 stores to $7ACC+X for X = 4-11), so the bytes written are $7AD0-$7AD7, row 21 column 18, the bottle's lower eight lines, left half.
Index base for the right half of the bottle's lower eight lines ($2D34 stores to $7AD4+X, X = 4-11: $7AD8-$7ADF, row 21 column 19).
Row 21, columns 20-23: the stairs and the wall at their foot.

Row 21, column 24, line 4: the telephone's handset on its table in the living room. While the phone rings (CTRL C sets $2B4C) $2ADB counts $2B4D down from $FF: above $80, every fourth count, bit 2 picks the raised or the resting drawing of lines 4-6 of columns 24-25 (the handset jumps) and the ring sound request $3566 is on; below $80 it rests. When he reaches the phone ($03C6 bit 7 set, $038D 4 or 5) $2AC1 blanks all six bytes and stops the ringing; the code at $2FFF-$300A clears lines 5-6 (handset lifted) and $3010-$301F draws it back at rest.
Row 21, column 24, line 5 of the telephone handset (rest $15, raised $10).
Row 21, column 24, line 6 of the telephone handset (rest $10, raised 0).
Row 21, column 25, line 4 of the telephone handset (rest 0, raised $50).
Row 21, column 25, line 5 of the telephone handset (rest $50, raised $10).
Row 21, column 25, line 6 of the telephone handset (rest $10, raised 0); line 7 is the table.

Row 21, columns 26-39: the purple easy chair (columns 26-29), the floor lamp, the fireplace (columns 32-35) with the fire (columns 33-34, rows 21-22: object 7, four flame frames or the empty grate, drawn by fire_flicker and fire_out through draw_object ($96ED)) and the front door (object 0).

Music driver work area, $7F40-$7FF9 (cleared by music_clear, $44E8, when a tune starts). This byte: offset of the next byte to read in the current voice's stream: music_fetch ($422C) reads ($53),Y with Y from here and increments it, music_commit ($405C) adds it to the stream pointer and zeroes it. The same memory is the letter buffer: the letter activity (22) assembles the letter's text here ($55C4-$55FF: 'Dear Friend,', the thank-you or the complaint paragraph, the sign-off, then $FF; at most 159 bytes, to $7FDE) and types it out through the pointer $66/$67 = $7F40 ($5599). It overwrites the voice state and most of sid_shadow, so the letter activity first turns the stereo off if it is playing (phases 1-6, ending with stereo_off).

Music driver: bits 4-6 of the op byte being executed (0-7), set by music_run_voice ($403A); the op handlers ($4082-$421D) use it as a sub-op or as the number of the voice field (zero page $55+n) to push, pop or load.

Music driver, vibrato and slide arithmetic: high byte of a 24-bit shift register ($7F42-$7F44). freq_shift ($4381) loads it with the voice's frequency shifted right Y times (this byte 0); freq_scale ($43A4) then shifts the register left once per bit of music_mul_factor, adding its top two bytes ($7F43 low, $7F42 high) into $4F/$50 for each set bit: the frequency change.
Middle byte of the vibrato/slide shift register: loaded with the frequency's high byte and shifted right in place with the low byte by freq_shift ($4390-$439C); freq_scale adds it into $4F.
Low byte of the vibrato/slide shift register: the frequency's low byte after the shift ($43A0).
Multiplier for the vibrato/slide product (freq_scale, $43A4): a depth from vibrato_shape ($4353) or a voice's slide multiplier (music_slide_mul), shifted out a bit at a time.

Voice 1's 13-byte state; voices 2 and 3 have the same layout at $7F73 and $7FA0 (offsets 0, $2D and $5A, from music_voice_offset $3FBC). music_timer_a copies it to zero page $53-$5F to work on the voice and back ($3F96-$3FAB). +0/+1 stream pointer (from tune_streams at start, music_voice_init $44A9); +2 current pitch, an index into freq_table (each note moves it up or down, $42C0-$42D2); +3 duration of the current note value; +4 articulation, the gate is released when the countdown falls to duration times this (2 at start); +5 tempo; +6 to +8 fields the stream can load and push (their use is not known); +9 countdown; +10 release point; +11 stack index; +12 status. Bytes 0-4 here.

Voice 1's tempo field (+5): the high byte of CIA1 timer A, $3B at start ($447E). music_set_tempo ($4183) stores a new value in all three voices' copies (this, $7F78, $7FA5) and in $DC05 with $DC04 = 0. $7F4C-$7F4E are voice 1's fields +6 to +8.

Countdown field (+9) of voice 1; indexed by the voice's block offset (music_cur_block_ofs) it serves all three voices ($7F4F, $7F7C, $7FA9). music_timer_a ($3F59) decrements it; at 0 the voice's next ops are read ($3F7B). A note sets it to eight times its duration ($4273).

Release point field (+10), indexed like music_v_countdown: when the countdown equals it and the gate is on, music_timer_a clears the gate bit ($3F62-$3F75). Set to duration times articulation ($4284). $7F51 is voice 1's stack index (+11).

Status field (+12) of voice 1, indexed for all voices: bit 7 the voice is playing ($C0 at start; cleared by the end op at $40F6), bit 6 the gate is on (set at every note, $424E-$4252), and the timer-B effects: bit 0 vibrato (fx_vibrato), bit 1 slide (fx_slide), bit 2 the slide's direction, bit 3 the voice's hook (fx_hook). music_timer_b ($3FC2) ORs the three voices' status bytes to see if any effect is on.

Voice 1's 32-byte stack ($7F53-$7F72), addressed through $60/$61 = block + 13 with the index at +11: return addresses of stream calls, loop counters and pushed fields (music_push $4235, music_pop $423C).
Voice 2's state block ($7F73-$7F7F, same layout as music_voice1): +0 to +4 here.
Voice 2's tempo field (+5), $3B at start ($4481), set with the others by music_set_tempo ($418A). $7F79-$7F7E are voice 2's fields +6 to +11.
Voice 2's status byte (+12); music_timer_b reads it directly ($3FC5) to see whether any voice has an effect enabled.
Voice 2's 32-byte stream stack ($7F80-$7F9F).
Voice 3's state block ($7FA0-$7FAC, same layout as music_voice1): +0 to +4 here.
Voice 3's tempo field (+5), $3B at start ($4484), set by music_set_tempo ($418D). $7FA6-$7FAB are voice 3's fields +6 to +11.
Voice 3's status byte (+12), read directly by music_timer_b ($3FC8).
Voice 3's 32-byte stream stack ($7FAD-$7FCC).

Shadow copy of the SID's 25 write-only registers $D400-$D418 ($7FCD-$7FE5), kept by the music driver so it can read values back. sid_init ($4547) loads it and the SID from sid_init_values ($4556) when a tune starts; sid_list_voice ($43FE), which the tunes call (op $C1 $FE $43 and a list address), writes register/value lists into both; notes write the voice's frequency ($42DC) at the voice's register offset (music_cur_sid_ofs); vibrato, slides and the sound jobs read the frequency back from here ($4393, $43CD, $45B2-$4677). This byte is voice 1's frequency low byte ($D400).

Shadow of $D401, voice 1's frequency high byte; with the register offset 7 or 14 it is voice 2's ($7FD5) or 3's ($7FDC). Written by notes ($42E6), fx_slide ($433B) and the sound jobs ($45C0, $45F7, $4609, $464C, $4667, $4691). $7FCF/$7FD0 shadow $D402/$D403 (voice 1 pulse width).

Shadow of $D404, voice 1's control register (waveform and gate); with the register offset, voices 2 and 3's ($7FD8, $7FDF). The gate bit is set at a note ($42F1-$42F9) and cleared at the release point ($3F6D-$3F75), by a gate-off note ($4297-$429F) and by the end op ($40FF). $7FD2/$7FD3 shadow $D405/$D406 (voice 1 attack/decay, sustain/release).

Shadow of $D407, voice 2's frequency low byte, used by name only in sound jobs 2 (job_v2_env3, $4599-$45AB) and 3 (job_all_fall, $45C6-$45CC). Job 3 writes the value it computes here to $D400, voice 1's register, instead of $D407 ($45CF).
Shadow of $D408, voice 2's frequency high byte (sound jobs 2 and 3: $45A6-$45AB, $45D4). $7FD6-$7FDA shadow $D409-$D40D (voice 2 pulse width, control, envelope).

Shadow of $D40E, voice 3's frequency low byte, swept down by sound jobs 3 (job_all_fall, $45DA-$45E8) and 5 (job_v3_fall, $4610-$4616). On a borrow job 3 decrements this byte and $D40E a second time ($45E8/$45EB) where the high byte would be expected.
Shadow of $D40F, voice 3's frequency high byte, decremented on a borrow by job_v3_fall ($461E). $7FDD-$7FE1 shadow $D410-$D414 (voice 3 pulse width, control, envelope).

Shadow of $D415, the filter cutoff's low bits. job_filter_env3 ($4574) puts voice 3's envelope output ($D41C) into the cutoff: the whole byte into $D416 and its low 3 bits into $D415, and stores both values here (the second store wins), so the shadow of $D416 is not kept up to date by it.

Shadow of $D416, the filter cutoff's high byte, written with $D416 by unused_filter_sweep ($3A99: INC $02F2, then store it). No JSR, JMP or pointer to $3A99 was found; whether a tune's call op reaches it is not known.
Shadow of $D417, filter resonance and routing: unused_filter_setup ($3A80) sets it and $D417 to $47; no caller of $3A80 has been found.

Shadow of $D418, filter mode and volume: unused_filter_setup ($3A88-$3A92) keeps the volume, sets band-pass (bit 5) and writes it here and to $D418. $7FE6 is cleared with the work area and otherwise unused.

The voice the music driver is working on, 0-2: the loop counter of music_timer_a ($3F40-$3FB3) and music_timer_b ($3FD1-$3FF6), read by music_note ($4245) and the effects ($4327, $433F, $4357, $4377).
The current voice's SID register offset, 0, 7 or 14 (from music_sid_offset, $3FB9): the index into sid_shadow and $D400 for its frequency and control bytes.
The current voice's state block offset, 0, $2D or $5A (from music_voice_offset, $3FBC): the index into music_voice1 and the base of the zero-page copy address ($3F7B-$3F94).
Three per-voice counters ($7FEA-$7FEC) incremented at every note (music_note, $4248, X = voice) along with note_count ($4789); no traced instruction reads them. play-02 holds $51, $81 and $10.

Three per-voice vibrato step counters ($7FED-$7FEF): fx_vibrato ($4357) increments the voice's counter on each timer-B tick; its low bits (AND music_vib_len - 1) index vibrato_shape ($4353: 0, 1, 3, 1) and bit music_vib_len chooses up or down ($4374-$437A).
Vibrato table length, 4 (set at $4447): music_vib_step AND (4 - 1) picks the vibrato_shape entry and AND 4 the direction.
Voice 1's slide multiplier, 7 at start ($4462); indexed by the voice ($432A) it serves all three ($7FF1-$7FF3). fx_slide scales the frequency change of a slide by it.
Voice 2's slide multiplier, 7 at start ($4465).
Voice 3's slide multiplier, 7 at start ($4468).

Voice 1's effect hook, a pointer (low byte here), $44A8 (an RTS) at start ($444C); indexed by voice times two ($4344-$434A) it serves all three ($7FF4, $7FF6, $7FF8). fx_hook ($433F) calls it through jmp_via_4f when bit 3 of the voice's status is set. unused_set_effect ($3A73), which nothing is known to call, points voice 1's hook at effect_nop ($3A96).
High byte of voice 1's effect hook ($44 at start, $4457; $3A when set by unused_set_effect).
Low byte of voice 2's effect hook, $A8 at start ($444F).
High byte of voice 2's effect hook, $44 at start ($445A).
Low byte of voice 3's effect hook, $A8 at start ($4452).
High byte of voice 3's effect hook, $44 at start ($445D): the last byte of the music driver's work area.
$7FFA-$7FFF: no traced instruction addresses these six bytes, the driver's clear loop stops at $7FF9 ($44F5, Y < $BA), no indexed access found reaches them, and they are 0 in every snapshot.

Entry points of the stereo's music driver, ten JMP-sized slots of three bytes. Four are live: music_tick_jmp ($800C), music_start_jmp ($800F), music_stop_jmp ($8012) and music_irq_jmp ($8018), each a JMP into the driver at $394E-$39B2 (its note engine is $3F3B-$46BC, its tunes are listed at tune_streams, $3A03, and its work area is $7F40-$7FF9). The other six slots, $8000, $8003, $8006, $8009, $8015 and $801B, hold RTS, NOP, NOP, and nothing in the image calls them. The piano uses the other sound driver, whose jump table is at $B000.

JMP sound_dispatch ($396E). The raster IRQ calls it once a frame ($0812) while music_playing ($801E) is non-zero, in place of the other sound driver's tick at $B003: runs the music driver's per-frame sound jobs, one for each bit set in sound_job_bits ($478D).

JMP music_driver_start ($394E): starts a tune on the stereo. Clears sound_job_bits and $02ED, then music_start ($4424) stops CIA1's timers and interrupts, clears the work area $7F40-$7FF9 (music_clear), loads 25 bytes of initial SID settings into sid_shadow and the SID (sid_init), rebuilds the note table freq_table ($46C9), points the three voices at the streams of tune music_tune ($478C, 0-3, chosen at random by activity 119) listed at tune_streams, and starts CIA1 timer A ($3B00 cycles, the note clock) and timer B ($4295 cycles, vibrato and slides) with interrupts. One caller: stereo_on ($9256), phase 5 of activity 120, in which he walks to the stereo (location 1) and puts a record on; it then sets music_playing.

JMP stop_music_timers ($39B2): CIA1 interrupt control $7F (all off), timer A and B control $08 (stopped). One caller: sound_requests ($347E), run from the main loop ($0974) when music_stop_req ($801F) is set.
Seventh slot of driver_jumps: RTS, NOP, NOP. No code in the image calls or jumps to $8015.

JMP timer_irq ($3959). The IRQ handler ($072C) calls it for every interrupt that is not the raster one, which in play means CIA1: timer A runs the music driver's notes (music_timer_a, $3F3B), timer B its vibrato and slides (music_timer_b, $3FBF).
Tenth and last slot of driver_jumps: RTS, NOP, NOP. Nothing in the image calls $801B.

Music playing flag: $FF while the stereo's music driver plays (set with turntable_on and act_music_on by stereo_on, $9264), 0 otherwise (cleared by stereo_off at $927C, in activities 18, 121 and 22, and by sound_requests at $3486 when a tune ends). Read by the raster IRQ ($080D: non-zero runs music_tick_jmp, zero runs the other driver's tick at $B003), by house_events ($2BC6: CTRL A does not start the alarm clock while music plays) and by the activity handlers at $E01A, $E0B7 and $E1A5.

Request to stop the music driver. Set to $FF by tune_end ($39AD), which every tune's own stream calls at its end (op $C1 $AD $39; it then falls into stop_music_timers), and to 1 by stereo_off ($9280). sound_requests ($3476, from the main loop at $0974) sees it, silences everything (sound_reset), calls music_stop_jmp, and clears it and music_playing.

Piano piece 1 of 4 (the table at $AB4E lists $8020, $838D, $85BA and $8730): Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, first movement (melody C5 E5 G5, B4 C5 D5 C5, A5 G5 C6 G5 over an Alberti bass C4 G4 E4 G4). Byte code of the sound driver at $B000, read by its interpreter at $D000: a note is two bytes, the pitch (high nibble 9-F = G, A, B, C, D, E, F; bit 3 raises it a semitone; bits 0-2 the octave; $10 is a rest) and an index into the duration table at $B726. Piece 1 (K. 545), voice 1's track: the accompaniment, calling patterns $80-$83 (two broken-chord figures and two short cadences) with a few held notes between; ends $00 at $8110, then a spare $00.

Piece 1 (K. 545), patterns $80-$83, used by voice 1: $80 and $83 are broken-chord (Alberti) figures, C4 G4 E4 G4 ... and G3 D4 B3 D4 ..., $81 and $82 short cadences; each starts with instrument $28 and ends with $21 (return).

Piece 1 (K. 545), patterns $84-$87, used by voice 3: the right-hand melody (C5 E5 G5, B4 C5 D5 C5, ... and the running scales), instrument $23; then two spare $00 bytes at $837B.

Piece 1 (K. 545), pattern table: eight words, the addresses of patterns $80-$87 ($8112, $8168, $817E, $8196, $8253, $82B3, $82F1, $8325). The header points here (header+12); the driver reads it at $D561-$D575.

Piece 4 (C-minor fugue), voice 1's track: long rests, then the subject in the bass (C4 B3 C4 G3 A-flat3 ...), 256 notes and rests; ends $00 at $8D97, then a spare $00 at $8D98.

An activity script that is only its $00 terminator. interrupt_for_request ($8FCD) and the code at $3100 and $33BD point the script pointer $0423/$0424 here, so that when the activity then running ends, script_next finds no follow-on activity. (The two bytes before it, $8D97-$8D98, are the end of piano_s4_v1.)

Music flag for the activity system: $FF while the stereo plays (set by stereo_on at $9261 with music_playing and turntable_on, cleared by stereo_off at $9276). When it is set, script_next ($8F46) resumes an interrupted activity straight away instead of chaining another pending request, and activity 15 ($916A) skips its request check.

The current activity number, 0-127, the index of the switch at $8DC6 (activity_table). Written by script_next (the next byte of the script at $0423/$0424, or 15 to resume after a request), by interrupt_for_request ($901C, the request's activity), by activity 15 ($919F, restoring saved_activity), by activity 0 ($E395, from the queue of typed-sentence actions) and at $30AB, $30F7 and $33B7. 1 while the activity for a CTRL-key request (the flags at $BEF3) is running, set by interrupt_for_request ($9011) and by activity 15 ($9184); 0 otherwise, cleared by script_next ($8F7F) when the request's script ends and at $904E. activity_dispatch's first call, $BED0, only picks up a new request while it is 0.

Activity number of the pending or running request, 0 for none. $BED0 sets it from the table at $BEE9 for the first request flag set at $BEF3-$BEFC; interrupt_for_request switches to it; script_next clears it ($8F82) and the request's flag when the request's activity ends. Copy of $039A made by interrupt_for_request ($8FE0) when a request interrupts an activity. Nothing reads it back: activity 15 restores the other saved values but not this one.
Copy of $038B made by interrupt_for_request ($8FDA). Like saved_039a, it is written and never read.
The interrupted activity's phase ($4C), saved by interrupt_for_request ($8FEB) and put back by activity 15 ($91A2).
The interrupted activity's number (activity, $8D9B), saved by interrupt_for_request ($8FE6) and put back by activity 15 ($919C).
The person's target location ($03C0) when a request interrupted him, saved at $8FF1 and restored by script_next ($8F5E) when the request's script ends.

Saved depth of the scratch location: location_depth_custom ($1DDA), saved at $9001 and restored at $8F6E, only when saved_target is $36.

High byte of the interrupted activity's script pointer ($0424), saved at $8FCA and put back by activity 15 ($9196).

The activity dispatcher, the last stage of the main loop ($09D5). Calls $BED0 (when no request is running, copies the activity of the first CTRL-key request flag set at $BEF3-$BEFC into request_activity), redraws the shade of the living-room floor lamp ($A93A writes lamp_colour to the colour matrix at $5F16/$5F17) when lamp_colour differs from the last value drawn ($A944), and calls house_events_call ($2A6E; house_events $2B54 takes the CTRL keys and animates the alarm clock, telephone, water cooler, television, stereo and stove). Then, only when the low three bits of $03C4 are clear, switches on the current activity: LDA activity, JSR switch_a ($3F13) with the 128-word activity_table after it.

The activity table: 128 words after the JSR $3F13 at $8DC6, each the address of an activity's handler minus one, indexed by the activity number (activity, $8D9B). Most handlers are themselves a JSR $3F11 switch on the phase $4C. Entries 0, 77 and 123-127 all lead to $E13F (activity 0, the chooser that starts queued actions and scheduled lists); 15 ($916A) resumes an interrupted activity; 78 ($AB1A) picks a piano piece and 79 ($E3CA) plays the piano; 114 is act114 ($8ED2) and 117 act117 ($8EC9). Entry 32 leads to $52D8, the byte after the font's last glyph. Side comments give each row's handler addresses.

Activity 117 (activity_table entry 117; in the script at $AAB2 used by activity 1): phase 0 is $93FF (X = $0C, then $94AE), phase 1 the shared handler $94CC, phase 2 script_next. The three words after the JSR are its switch table.
Switch table of act117 (three words after its JSR $3F11, handlers minus one): phase 0 $93FF, phase 1 $94CC, phase 2 script_next ($8F0E).

Switch handler used by five tables (activities 22, 120, 121, 18 and 118): target location 1, the stereo, then next phase (A = 1, set_target_next).

Close, from 7: op_goto_spot, walk_sub_take_requests, op_reach_close, op_start_close, op_wait_step, op_unreach, $8F0B. Open in place, from 14: op_start_open, op_wait_plain, $8F0B. Close in place, from 17: op_start_close, op_wait_plain, $8F0B.
Three bytes, $1D $1E $1F, after object_op's 20-entry table; no reference to them was found (no stub sets $68 above 17).

Exits of getup_step, placed before its entry: $9502 goes to the next phase, $9505 returns until the next call. $94FD (pose $08 through set_pose) is reached only by the BEQ at $951B, which cannot be taken: Y is 4 there and is compared with 6.

Phase handler that stands the person up again, one pose step per 8 calls (op_divider): find his pose in pose_steps and step back up the list, $20 or $1F -> $1E -> $21 -> $08; when the pose is $08, or not in the list, go to the next phase. Follows rummaging and closing low objects.
Is object X one of the low ones, 8-11 (the drawers of the phone table, nightstand, dresser and filing cabinet), that he crouches for? Returns A = 0 and Z set for 8-11, A = 1 otherwise.
The RTS of is_low_object. getup_step reads it as the base $9531,Y with Y >= 1, i.e. pose_steps[Y-1].
Poses for crouching down to a low object and standing up again: $08 (standing), $21, $1E, $1F, $20, then 0 ending the list and one more 0.
Find the person's pose $038B in pose_steps: returns Y = index + 1, or Y = 6 with A = $08 when it is not in the list.
Part of op_reach_open: from pose $1E set $1F, reload X with obj_current, next sub-phase.

Object step (open), once every 8 calls (op_divider): for a door or cupboard set pose $19 and $47AA := 10, next sub-phase ($9593). For a low object step down pose_steps (a pose not in the list starts at $21), and at $1E set $1F and go on (op_crouched).
Object step (close), once every 8 calls: for a door as op_reach_open; for a low object go on once the pose is $20, set $20 from $1E, otherwise step down pose_steps.
Object step: a low object goes straight on. For a door count $47AA down, one per call, and at 0 set pose $08 and go on: he holds pose $19 for 10 calls.
Next sub-phase: INC $68. Used by many $68 machines inside and outside this range.

Object step: set the walk target for object X to its spot obj_spot[X] (a location number); for the low objects 8-11 the location is copied into the scratch location $36 ($16AE) and $36 becomes the target. For the other objects nothing changes if the target already is that location. Then next sub-phase.

Sub-phase handler, the $68-level twin of $8FA7, also used by the $68 machines at $21B5 and $31E6. Unless $0391 is non-zero, when he is standing or arrived ($03BC 0, 3 or 6) and a request is pending ($8D9E): with no interruption running, save the context and switch to it ($8FC1); with one running, switch only if the first set request flag belongs to another activity (start_request_a). Otherwise return while $03BC is non-zero and go to the next sub-phase when he has arrived.
Object step: if object X is not closed, state := 3 (half open, closing), obj_timer[X] := 8, next sub-phase and redraw (draw_object); if it is closed already, skip this and the wait step.
Object step: if object X is closed, state := 1 (half open), sound request $355E := 1, obj_timer[X] := 8, next sub-phase and redraw; if it is not closed, skip this and the wait step.
Part of op_wait_step: one call before the state changes (timer 1), a low object switches the person between the two crouched poses $1F and $20.

Object step: count obj_timer[X] down (op_arm_toggle while it runs); at 0 advance the state, (state + 1) & 3, so 1 -> 2 (open) and 3 -> 0 (closed, with sound request $355F := 1), redraw and go to the next sub-phase.
Count $47AA up and return its low 3 bits: zero once in 8 calls. op_reach_open, op_reach_close and getup_step act only then.

Draw house object X (0-15) in its current state: patches the colour-matrix address obj_scr into the STA at $3E8A and the colour-RAM address obj_col into the STA at $3E96, points $18/$19 at the object's frame list (obj_frames), takes entry obj_state[X] of the list into the operand of copy_frame_record, which loads the 6-byte frame record into $18-$1D, sets the bitmap address $1E/$1F from obj_bmp, Y := obj_width and X := obj_rows_m1, and draws the rows (draw_rows).

Called from $2CA7 on every main-loop pass while $2B49 (the fire's remaining burn count) is non-zero. $AF8B, phase 25 of activity 7, adds 1 to that count; parser rules $C98A (LIGHT/START/MAKE/BURN/IGNITE with FIRE), $C99A (YOU with SEEM/LOOK/APPEAR and CHILLY/COLD) and $C9AA (PLAY/PERFORM/USE/TRY with FIRE) name activity 7. Every 8th pass ($09DB & 7 = 0) pick a random flame frame 0-3, one higher (mod 4) if it equals fire_state, store it and redraw the fire (object 7).
Called from $2CC6 when the burn count $2B49 runs out: fire_state := 4, the empty-grate frame, and redraw object 7.

The petting animation, called from $2CCE on every main-loop pass while the phase $2B46 is non-zero; counts $2B47 down and acts on every 4th count. Phase 3: the arm (object 14) comes out, frames 0-3, redrawn every 8 counts, then phase 2 with $2B47 := $20. Phase 2: the hand (object 15) pats, its two frames alternating every 8 counts, and every 16 counts $3577 := 0 and $3576 := 1; then phase 1 with $2B47 := $18. Phase 1: the arm goes back in, frames 3-0, then phase 0. CTRL P with the person at the easy chair starts it, or lengthens or reverses it ($2C3C-$2C7C).

How upper_body_new_target picks the next target frame of the upper body (head and shoulders). Bits 0-1: how far the head may turn from the body (target offset 0..+2 notches; 0 lets $0414 choose); bits 2-3: bit 3 set turns to the other side (0 lets chance choose); bits 5-6: the head row (0 lets chance choose, with row 1 when that is 0 too); bit 7: use the row as it is, without the random nudge. Decremented by every command dispatch ($D357); the dispatch that brings it to 0 goes through snd_rare_path. sound_frame steps its low three bits each frame, 0 to 4 and back to 0 ($B516-$B527), and it is mixed into snd_random ($B2EB, $B530).

Per channel, index 2 x channel (0-10): frames left with the key down. Loaded with snd_note_off from the duration table snd_durations after a note ($D0A6-$D0AF); counted down by sound_frame ($B571-$B58A).
Per channel (2 x channel): frames of release after the key-up. When snd_note_on is 0 each frame decrements this one and clears the key bit; when both are 0 the channel reads its next command.

Per channel (2 x channel): non-zero while the channel plays. A tune start stores the stream address's low OR high byte ($B293); the end of the stream stores 0 ($B5FB). snd_output gives a SID voice to the set-A channel when it is active, else to set B. play-01 has $81, $85, $89 for channels 3-5: tune 12 running from $8100, $8104, $8108.

Per channel (2 x channel): the last command byte read ($D006). When a stream ends and this is non-zero, sound_frame clears it, marks a set-A channel in snd_ended_a and releases the SID voice's key once ($B5FE-$B627).

Shadow SID registers, seven bytes a channel (frequency low and high, pulse low and high, control, attack/decay, sustain/release) for channels 0-5 at $B031, $B038, $B03F, $B046, $B04D, $B054 (offsets in snd_reg_offsets). snd_output copies them to $D400-$D414. This byte: frequency low.
snd_regs + 1, frequency high byte (per channel, seven-byte stride). Written by notes ($D08C) and slides ($D230-$D252).
snd_regs + 2, pulse width low byte; with the next four bytes loaded from an instrument by snd_set_instrument.
snd_regs + 3, pulse width high nibble; changed by the pulse sweep at $D2B5.

snd_regs + 4, the voice control register: bit 0 key (gate), set by a note's duration ($D0B9) and cleared at the key-up ($B590); bit 3 (test) is written to the SID once and then cleared by snd_output ($B4D4-$B4E5).

Filter record of set A, five bytes ($B05B-$B05F; set B's is at $B062): cutoff low bits for $D415 with bit 7 meaning 'write pending', cutoff high byte ($D416), resonance and voice routing ($D417), mode and volume ($D418), and a one-shot flag. Loaded from snd_filter_presets ($D362) and swept by $D258; written to the SID by snd_output ($B46A-$B4BD). The talking syllables load the band-pass presets 11-14 here.
Filter record of set A: cutoff high byte, written to $D416.
Filter record of set A: resonance (high nibble) and voice routing (low bits), written to $D417.
Filter record of set A: filter mode and volume, written to $D418.

Filter record of set A, last byte: non-zero ($FF from a tune start) makes snd_output write the record once, then zero its first byte (the pending bit with the cutoff low bits) and this flag; 0 (after $D362) keeps it pending, so it is rewritten every frame and set B's record is not written ($72 = $FF).

Filter record of set B, the same five bytes as snd_filter_a ($B062-$B066). snd_output uses it when the voice it is writing belongs to set B (register offset $15 or more). The end of a note with snd_filter_restore set marks it pending again ($B5A5).
Per channel (2 x channel): non-zero while music command 2's repeat is running ($D0F3-$D135). Paired with snd_loop1_count.
Per channel: repeats left for music command 2 (loop back to the given address n times).
Per channel: non-zero while music command $22's repeat is running ($D42B-$D443), a second loop level.
Per channel: repeats left for music command $22.
Per channel: return address, low byte, of a stream subroutine called with music command 4 ($D11A); non-zero with snd_return_hi means 'return here when the called stream ends' ($B5D0-$B5E7).
Per channel: return address, high byte, for music command 4. Cleared on the return.
Seven bytes a channel: the caller's shadow registers saved by music command 4 ($D10B-$D115) and put back into snd_regs when the subroutine's stream ends ($B5EE-$B5F6).

Per channel: when non-zero at the end of a note, set B's filter record is marked pending again ($B5A0-$B5AA). Cleared at a tune start and at the end of a note; no instruction found sets it non-zero. snd_output also skips a set-B channel while it is set ($B44D).
Per channel: the release count, copied on each release frame ($B57B); non-zero when the note ends means it had a release ($B59B), then cleared.
Per channel (set A only, index below 6): set to $FF when the channel's stream ends ($B60E). Nothing found reads it.

Per channel: pitch slide step, low byte; read from the stream by snd_read_slide or set to $FF with the high byte by music command 7 ($D474), which makes the slides at $D1CB/$D1CF derive the step from the current frequency.
Per channel: pitch slide step, high byte (bit 7 set: use the low seven bits as they are, $D1E8).
Incremented every frame by sound_frame ($B52A); a source of variation for snd_random and for the automatic slide step ($D1F0).
Incremented only in snd_rare_path, when snd_dispatch_count reaches 0 during a dispatch; its wrap to 0 triggers the rare branch there. $01 or $02 in the snapshots.

The driver's random byte: mixed from snd_frame_count, snd_dispatch_count and snd_frame_mix every frame ($B52A-$B539) and at each tune start ($B2E8-$B2EE). Music command $20 ($D396-$D3A8) ANDs it with its mask operand and adds its base operand to choose which stream subroutine to call: this is where the talking sound's random syllables and phrases come from.
Seven bytes a channel: the shadow registers saved by music command $0A ($D487-$D491) and put back by command $0B ($D4C1).
Per channel: return address, low byte, saved by music command $0A ($D496) and used by command $0B ($D4B3).
Per channel: return address, high byte, for music commands $0A and $0B.

At $B10B + 7 x channel: two bits of key-down tracking. snd_output forms (state x 2 + key bit) AND 7 and calls the handler from snd_track_handlers, so every second key-down flips snd_toggle_ch3 or snd_toggle_ch45.
At $B10C + 7 x channel: pulse, control and envelope bytes saved by music command $20 ($D38A-$D394) and put back by command $21 ($D3D5-$D3DD).
Per channel: return address, low byte, saved by music command $20 ($D3B2) and used by command $21 ($D3C7).
Per channel: return address, high byte, for music commands $20 and $21.
Per channel: return address, low byte, saved by music command $24 ($D4FD) and used by command $25 ($D51A).
Per channel: return address, high byte, for music commands $24 and $25.
